answer: Yes. The private router (`private.router`, the endpoints in `app/api/routes/private.py`) is only included when `settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local"`. The `ENVIRONMENT` setting in `app/core/config.py` controls it. The login, users, utils and items routers are always mounted.

Make sure the PR has exactly one of these labels: breaking, security, feature, bug, refactor, upgrade, docs, lang-all, internal. The check-labels job uses label-checker with `one_of`. It fails if the PR has none of them, or more than one. The labeler action may add a label automatically. If it didn't, add one yourself. Adding or removing a label re-runs the check.

Operation IDs are generated by `custom_generate_unique_id` in backend/app/main.py. It's passed to `FastAPI(generate_unique_id_function=...)` and returns `"{first tag}-{route function name}"`, for example `items-read_items`. Every route therefore needs at least one tag, because `route.tags[0]` is used. On the frontend, `openapi-ts.config.ts` uses the first tag to name the service class: `classNameBuilder` is `{{name}}Service`, so you get `ItemsService`. Its `methodNameBuilder` strips the service-name prefix from the operation name and lowercases the first letter, so the method is `readItems`.

Publishing a GitHub release (release event, type `published`) triggers the "Deploy to Production" workflow. It runs on a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner labelled `production`. The job is skipped in the main fastapi repository (`github.repository_owner != 'fastapi'`).
90% minimum backend coverage. The backend CI job runs `coverage report --fail-under=90`, so it fails below 90%. The smokeshow workflow also sets a coverage threshold of 90.

A pre-commit hook named `add-release-date` runs `uv run python scripts/add_latest_release_date.py` whenever release-notes.md is changed. The script finds the first header that matches `## X.Y.Z`. If that header has no `(…)` part, it rewrites the line as `## X.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)` using `date.today().isoformat()`. If the header already has a date, it leaves it alone. If no header matches, it exits with status 1.
8 days. The login endpoint builds its token with ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES, which is set to 60 * 24 * 8 = 11,520 minutes.

A pydantic model validator on Settings (`_enforce_non_default_secrets`) calls `_check_default_secret` for SECRET_KEY, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD. If any of them is still "changethis", it only emits a warning when ENVIRONMENT is "local". In any other environment it raises a ValueError, so the app won't start.

The API won't boot. With ENVIRONMENT=staging and SECRET_KEY="changethis", the Settings model validator `_enforce_non_default_secrets` calls `_check_default_secret`. Because the environment isn't "local", that call raises a ValueError: 'The value of SECRET_KEY is "changethis", for security, please change it, at least for deployments.' Settings fails to load at import time. Only ENVIRONMENT=local gets a warning instead. POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD are checked the same way.

The backend pre-start check (`backend_pre_start.py`, run on container start) makes up to 300 attempts (`max_tries = 60 * 5`, which is 5 minutes). It waits a fixed 1 second between attempts (`wait_seconds = 1`, via tenacity `wait_fixed`). The separate compose healthcheck on the db service (`pg_isready`) is different: it uses `retries: 5` and `interval: 10s`.

No. A superuser cannot delete their own account through the users endpoints. DELETE /users/me returns 403 "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves" when current_user.is_superuser is true. The admin delete-user-by-id route has the same check (users.py:226).
You need at least 90% coverage. The backend CI job runs `coverage report --fail-under=90`, so it fails below 90%.

The operationId will be "orders-<function_name>", which is the first tag, a hyphen, then the endpoint function's name. For example, a function named `read_order` gets "orders-read_order". The app sets `custom_generate_unique_id` as the `generate_unique_id_function` on `FastAPI(...)`, and it returns `f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"`. `route.name` defaults to the function name.

GET /items/ returns an ItemsPublic object, `{data: [...ItemPublic], count}`. A superuser gets every item in the database, and `count` is the total number of items. A normal user gets only the items where `owner_id` is their own id, and `count` covers only those items. Both are sorted by `created_at` descending, so the newest come first. Both are paginated with `skip` (default 0) and `limit` (default 100). `count` is the total before pagination.

The token is kept in the browser's localStorage under the key "access_token". useAuth.ts sets it after login. main.tsx configures OpenAPI.TOKEN to read it for each request. When any query or mutation fails with an ApiError of status 401 or 403, handleApiError removes "access_token" from localStorage and redirects the browser to /login with window.location.href.
8 days (ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 60 * 24 * 8 = 11,520 minutes). The login route uses this value to set the access token's expiry.

The generated client only contains PrivateService if the OpenAPI schema it was generated from included the private routes. The backend registers the private router only when settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local". If the client is generated against a non-local backend (staging or production), the private endpoints are absent from the schema. `PrivateService` is then missing from src/client, and the import in privateApi.ts fails.

From the project root run `bash ./scripts/generate-client.sh` (with the backend venv active), then commit the changes. The script does the following: (1) `cd backend` and use `uv run python` to import `app.main` and dump `app.main.app.openapi()` as JSON to `openapi.json`; (2) move `openapi.json` into `frontend/`; (3) run `bun run --filter frontend generate-client`, which runs `openapi-ts` (@hey-api/openapi-ts, configured in `frontend/openapi-ts.config.ts` with input `./openapi.json`) to generate the client in `frontend/src/client`; (4) run `bun run lint` to format and lint the generated code. The manual alternative is to download `/api/v1/openapi.json` into `frontend/openapi.json` and run `bun run generate-client`.

The /admin route (frontend/src/routes/_layout/admin.tsx) has a beforeLoad guard. It calls UsersService.readUserMe() and, if the user isn't a superuser, throws redirect({ to: "/" }). The sidebar also only shows the Admin link to superusers (AppSidebar.tsx:23, `currentUser?.is_superuser`).

Yes. In corpus/frontend/playwright.config.ts, the `CI` env var changes five settings:
- `forbidOnly` is on (line 17), so a committed `test.only` fails the run.
- `retries` is 2 on CI and 0 locally (line 19).
- `workers` is 1 on CI and Playwright's default locally (line 21).
- `reporter` is `blob` on CI and `html` locally (line 23).
- `reuseExistingServer` is off on CI and on locally (line 89), so CI always starts a fresh web server.

An admin (superuser) sees everybody's items, not just their own. The Items page calls GET /items/ (`read_items`) with skip=0 and limit=100. For a superuser, the query has no owner filter. Non-admin users only get items where `owner_id` matches their own id. Both cases return items ordered by `created_at` descending, so the newest come first. The count is calculated with the same filter. Results are paginated with skip and limit, and the frontend asks for the first 100.

Traefik routes by hostname, built from the DOMAIN variable: backend → api.${DOMAIN}, frontend → dashboard.${DOMAIN}, Adminer → adminer.${DOMAIN}. Each has HTTP and HTTPS routers. (The Traefik dashboard itself is traefik.${DOMAIN}.)

Give the runner the label `production`. GitHub adds `self-hosted` automatically, and the job requires both. The job runs when a GitHub release is published (`release` event, type `published`). It is skipped in repositories owned by `fastapi`.

The backend service runs `curl -f http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check/` as its healthcheck. It runs every 10s with a 5s timeout and 5 retries. I confirmed the block sits in the backend service by its position beside the backend build, env and labels. I didn't read the service name line itself.
About 5 minutes: it retries once per second, up to 300 attempts (max_tries = 60 * 5, wait_seconds = 1), then fails.
By default the backend image runs the FastAPI server in production mode with 4 workers: `fastapi run --workers 4 app/main.py`.
When CI is set, Playwright uses the 'blob' reporter, which can be merged across shards, and 2 retries. Locally it uses the 'html' reporter with 0 retries.

The public Traefik gets its certificates from Let's Encrypt through an ACME resolver named "le". The resolver is set up with the registration email from `EMAIL` and uses the TLS-ALPN challenge (`tlschallenge=true`). Routers opt in with `tls.certresolver=le`. Traefik writes the certificates to `/certificates/acme.json`. That path is on the named Docker volume `traefik-public-certificates`, so the certificates survive container recreation.
Run `docker compose watch`. The frontend is at http://localhost:5173 and the backend API is at http://localhost:8000. Swagger docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs.

The browser keeps your session in localStorage, under the key `access_token`. It's a JWT bearer token, not a cookie. It's written at login in useAuth.ts:45 and sent with each API request through `OpenAPI.TOKEN` (main.tsx:17-19). The kick-out is the global `handleApiError` handler in main.tsx. Any query or mutation that fails with an ApiError of status 401 or 403 makes it remove `access_token` and set `window.location.href = "/login"`. So an expired or invalid token, or a 403 from the API, sends you back to login. Logout in useAuth.ts:57 also removes the token. useAuth.ts:15 treats a missing token as logged out.

Open the Mailcatcher web UI at http://localhost:1080. With Docker Compose locally, the backend sends SMTP to the mailcatcher service on port 1025. Mailcatcher captures every email, including password recovery ones, and shows them in that web interface instead of sending them.
The link is valid for 48 hours (EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS = 48). It opens the frontend `/reset-password` page, with the token in the query string: `{FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token=...`.

After deploying, open the dashboard (frontend) at https://dashboard.<DOMAIN> and the API at https://api.<DOMAIN>. For example, with DOMAIN=fastapi-project.example.com the dashboard is https://dashboard.fastapi-project.example.com and the API base URL is https://api.fastapi-project.example.com. The API docs are at https://api.fastapi-project.example.com/docs. A staging deploy adds `staging.` to the domain, e.g. https://dashboard.staging.fastapi-project.example.com. These hostnames come from the Traefik rules in compose.yml, which use Host(`dashboard.${DOMAIN}`) and Host(`api.${DOMAIN}`).

The Admin sidebar item is only added for superusers (AppSidebar checks `currentUser?.is_superuser`), so your account isn't a superuser. If you go to /admin directly, the route's `beforeLoad` fetches your user with `readUserMe()`. If `is_superuser` is false, it throws `redirect({ to: "/" })` and sends you to the home page. The backend also rejects non-superusers on superuser-only endpoints.
docker compose exec backend bash scripts/tests-start.sh

We use Argon2 (via pwdlib; Argon2Hasher is listed first, so it's the default for new hashes). Bcrypt is kept only as a legacy fallback. Accounts with old bcrypt hashes still log in normally. On a successful login, `verify_and_update` returns a new Argon2 hash. `crud.authenticate` saves it to the user's `hashed_password` and commits. Accounts that never log in keep their bcrypt hashes. Argon2 hashes are not rewritten on login.

No. The /password-recovery/{email} endpoint returns the same message whether or not the email is registered ("If that email is registered, we sent a password recovery link"). It only sends the email if the user exists. The separate superuser-only /password-recovery-html-content endpoint does return a 404 for unknown emails, but it requires superuser authentication.

Mostly no. crud.authenticate runs verify_password against a DUMMY_HASH when the email isn't found, so unknown and known emails take about the same time. The login endpoint returns the same "Incorrect email or password" error for both. Minor residual differences (legacy bcrypt rehash commit, and a hard-coded Argon2 dummy hash that must match the real parameters) are not practical leaks.

A staging deployment is triggered by a push (or merge) to the `master` branch. The "Deploy to Staging" GitHub Actions workflow runs on a self-hosted runner labeled `staging`. It builds and starts the stack with docker compose (`build`, then `up -d`). It is skipped when the repository owner is `fastapi`, so it only runs in user projects.

No. Sentry is initialised only when SENTRY_DSN is set and settings.ENVIRONMENT != "local". ENVIRONMENT defaults to "local" for development, so local backend runs don't send errors to Sentry. Staging and production do, provided a DSN is configured. I didn't open config.py to confirm the default in code. The default comes from deployment.md, which says ENVIRONMENT is "by default `local`".

Dependabot checks GitHub Actions daily. It checks the uv (Python), bun, Docker (/backend and /frontend) and Docker Compose ecosystems weekly. The only exclusion is the bun ecosystem's ignore entry for the `@hey-api/openapi-ts` dependency, so Dependabot won't open PRs for it.

The suite is split into 4 parallel shards. test-playwright uses a matrix with shardIndex [1,2,3,4] and shardTotal [4], with fail-fast off. Each shard runs `playwright test --shard=N/4` inside docker compose. Each shard uploads a blob report. A merge-playwright-reports job then combines them into one HTML report.

The tests don't run at all when the `changes` job (dorny/paths-filter) finds no changes in backend/**, frontend/**, .env, compose*.yml or .github/workflows/playwright.yml. In that case test-playwright is skipped, because its condition is `needs.changes.outputs.changed == 'true'`. The merge job is skipped too. The alls-green-playwright check still passes, because it lists test-playwright under allowed-skips.

The backend lint script runs four checks on `app`. `mypy app` does type checking. `ty check app` does a second type check with ty. `ruff check app` does lint rules. `ruff format app --check` verifies formatting without changing files. The script uses `set -e`, so it stops at the first failure.

The API accepts cross-origin requests from the origins in `BACKEND_CORS_ORIGINS`, plus `FRONTEND_HOST`. `BACKEND_CORS_ORIGINS` is a comma-separated list of URLs and defaults to empty. `FRONTEND_HOST` defaults to http://localhost:5173. Trailing slashes are stripped from the configured origins. `CORSMiddleware` in main.py receives this combined list as `allow_origins`.

Certificates are issued by Let's Encrypt via Traefik's ACME resolver "le" (TLS challenge, email from $EMAIL). They're stored in /certificates/acme.json, which is on the named volume traefik-public-certificates. Recreating the Traefik container does not lose them, because the volume persists. They would be lost only if the volume were deleted, for example with `docker compose down -v`.

The session token is not in an httpOnly cookie. It is stored in `localStorage` under the key "access_token", so any JavaScript on the page can read it. That includes injected scripts if there is an XSS bug. After login it is saved with `localStorage.setItem("access_token", ...)` in `useAuth.ts`. It is attached to API requests through `OpenAPI.TOKEN`, which reads it from `localStorage` in `main.tsx`.

It is removed in two cases:
1. On logout, `logout()` in `useAuth.ts` calls `localStorage.removeItem("access_token")` and redirects to /login.
2. When any API query or mutation returns a 401 or 403, `handleApiError` in `main.tsx` (lines 21-26) removes it and redirects to /login.

I found no other code that clears the token. It has no cookie-style expiry and persists across browser restarts until one of the two cases above happens. It is also not cleared when the tab closes.

The user's items are deleted along with the user (cascade delete). `User.items` is declared with `cascade_delete=True`, and `Item.owner_id` is a foreign key with `ondelete="CASCADE"`. The admin delete endpoint in users.py also explicitly runs `delete(Item).where(Item.owner_id == user_id)` before it deletes the user.
UUIDs. Records use `uuid.UUID` primary keys generated with `uuid.uuid4`. The User and Item models both do this. An Alembic migration converted the old integer IDs to UUIDs.

It raises an HTTPException with status 403 Forbidden and detail "Could not validate credentials". jwt.decode raises InvalidTokenError for an expired or tampered token, and a payload that fails validation raises ValidationError. Both are caught and turned into this response.

If SECRET_KEY isn't set in the environment or .env, Settings generates a random value with `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`. This is a new random key on each process start. It is not the "changethis" placeholder that the README and deployment docs mention. The validator at line 110 only checks the value for that placeholder.

After a successful login, `authenticate` calls `verify_password`, which uses pwdlib's `verify_and_update`. For a legacy bcrypt hash this returns a new Argon2 hash. `authenticate` then overwrites `db_user.hashed_password` with it, commits, and refreshes the user. The bcrypt hash is replaced by an Argon2 hash. If the password is wrong, nothing changes.

The `emails_enabled` computed property in the settings. It is true only when both `SMTP_HOST` and `EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL` are set to non-empty values. `send_email` in `backend/app/utils.py` asserts this, and user creation in `users.py` checks it before sending.

Defaults (config.py): SMTP_TLS=True, SMTP_SSL=False, SMTP_PORT=587, SMTP_HOST/USER/PASSWORD=None, EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL/NAME=None. (compose.override.yml sets SMTP_TLS "false" for the local mail catcher.) If both SMTP_TLS and SMTP_SSL are true, TLS wins. In send_email, `if settings.SMTP_TLS: ... elif settings.SMTP_SSL:` means only tls=True is set and SSL is ignored.

Every password field in the request models has a minimum length of 8 and a maximum length of 128 characters. This covers `password` on user create and register, `current_password` and `new_password` on password change, and `new_password` on password reset. The optional `password` on user update has the same limits, but it can also be None. All of these are defined in `corpus/backend/app/models.py`; the line cited is the first one (line 23).

It rejects the request with an HTTP 409 Conflict and the detail "User with this email already exists". It looks up the new email, and if that account has a different id from the current user, it raises the error before anything is updated or committed. If the email is the user's own, there is no conflict.

A 403 Forbidden response with the body {"detail": "Not enough permissions"}. GET, PUT and DELETE all do the same check. If the item doesn't exist, they return 404 "Item not found" instead. Superusers skip the ownership check.

PATCH /users/me/password returns HTTP 400 in two cases. "Incorrect password" means the current password is wrong. "New password cannot be the same as the current one" means the new password equals the current one. Authentication failures from the CurrentUser dependency and 422 validation errors on the body can also occur. I didn't read those dependency or schema definitions.

Yes. POST /api/v1/users/signup (register_user) is public and needs no login. It creates a new user from a UserRegister body. If the email is already taken, it rejects the request with HTTP 400 and the detail "The user with this email already exists in the system". It creates nothing in that case.

From the top-level project directory (with the backend virtualenv activated), run `bash ./scripts/generate-client.sh`. It dumps the app's OpenAPI schema to openapi.json, moves it into frontend/, and runs `bun run --filter frontend generate-client` (openapi-ts) to regenerate frontend/src/client. Then commit the changes. Manual alternative: save http://localhost/api/v1/openapi.json as frontend/openapi.json and run `bun run generate-client` in frontend.

The backend tests use a session-scoped, autouse pytest fixture named `db`. It opens a Session and runs `init_db(session)`. After the whole test session finishes, it runs `delete(Item)` and then `delete(User)` to wipe both tables, and commits. Nothing is cleaned between individual tests or modules.

The recovery email doesn't go to a real inbox. It is caught by the Mailcatcher container (schickling/mailcatcher) that runs in the local Docker Compose stack. You can read it in Mailcatcher's web UI at http://localhost:1080. The backend service in compose.override.yml sends it there with SMTP_HOST="mailcatcher", SMTP_PORT="1025" and SMTP_TLS="false", and EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL is "noreply@example.com". No SMTP user or password is set. Mailcatcher's SMTP port 1025 is also published on localhost.

The names come from the backend's FastAPI operationIds plus the hey-api sdk plugin config. FastAPI's custom_generate_unique_id (backend/app/main.py:10-11) makes operationId "<first tag>-<route function name>", e.g. "items-read_items" (router tag "items"). In frontend/openapi-ts.config.ts the @hey-api/sdk plugin uses asClass + operationId: the tag becomes the class via classNameBuilder "{{name}}Service" (items -> ItemsService), and methodNameBuilder strips the service-name prefix from the operation name (itemsReadItems -> ReadItems) and lowercases the first letter -> readItems.

No, it doesn't validate the token. The `/_layout` route's `beforeLoad` guard calls `isLoggedIn()` and redirects to `/login` if that returns false. `isLoggedIn()` only checks that `access_token` exists in localStorage (`localStorage.getItem("access_token") !== null`). It doesn't check the token's signature, its expiry or whether the server accepts it. A bad or expired token still gets past the guard. The backend enforces real validity when the pages make API calls and get 401/403 responses.

A logged-in user is redirected to "/" (the home page). Both /login and /signup run a beforeLoad guard that checks isLoggedIn() (an access token is present) and throws redirect({ to: "/" }). The login page is shown only to logged-out users. The same guard is on recover-password and reset-password.

If the URL has no token (missing or non-string, which the zod schema turns into ""), the route's beforeLoad throws a redirect to /login, so the reset form never renders. A logged-in user is redirected to "/" first, before the token check.

The email link is f"{settings.FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token={token}". With the default FRONTEND_HOST of http://localhost:5173, that is http://localhost:5173/reset-password?token=<jwt>. The token is valid for EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS, which defaults to 48 hours (2 days).

A first-time visitor gets the "dark" theme. main.tsx wraps the app in <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="dark" storageKey="vite-ui-theme">, which overrides the provider's own default of "system". When the theme is changed, setTheme writes it to the browser's localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme". On load, the provider reads that key first and only uses the default if nothing is stored.

The DataTable offers 5, 10, 25 and 50 rows per page. The whole pagination footer is shown only when `table.getPageCount() > 1`, meaning the data spans more than one page at the current page size. The footer holds the "Showing X to Y of N entries" text, the Rows per page selector, the "Page X of Y" label and the first/previous/next/last buttons.

Creating an item invalidates only the ["items"] query key, in the mutation's onSettled, so it runs on success or error. Deleting an item calls queryClient.invalidateQueries() with no key, so every cached query is invalidated and refetched, not just items. That includes users and currentUser.

Each mutation sets `onError: handleError.bind(showErrorToast)`. `handleError` calls `extractErrorMessage(err)` and passes the result to `showErrorToast`, which is the `this` function. `extractErrorMessage` returns `err.message` for an AxiosError. Otherwise it reads `err.body.detail`. If `detail` is an array, it uses the first item's `.msg`. If `detail` is missing or empty, it falls back to "Something went wrong."

No. The code looks like it branches on `is_superuser`, but both branches give the same tabs. `tabsConfig` has three tabs: My profile, Password and Danger zone. Superusers get `tabsConfig.slice(0, 3)`, which returns all three. Other users get `tabsConfig`, which is also all three.
No. The profile form limits full name to 30 characters (z.string().max(30)). The API allows up to 255 (max_length=255 on full_name in the backend models, including UserUpdateMe).

UserActionsMenu deliberately returns null when the row's user id equals the logged-in user's id (from useAuth). This hides the edit/delete actions on your own row, so admins can't edit or delete themselves from the admin table.

For an admin (superuser), the API rejects the request. DELETE /users/me returns HTTP 403 with detail "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves", and nothing is deleted. In the app, the mutation's onError runs handleError, which shows that detail message in an error toast. The success path (success toast and logout()) does not run, so the admin stays logged in on the settings page. onSettled only invalidates the "currentUser" query.

The `db` service runs `postgres:18`. Its healthcheck is `pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d ${POSTGRES_DB}`, run every 10s with a 10s timeout, 5 retries and a 30s start period. The data is stored in the named Docker volume `app-db-data`, which is mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata`. `PGDATA` is set to the same path.

The prestart service uses the backend image and runs `bash scripts/prestart.sh`. That script does three things in order: (1) `python app/backend_pre_start.py`, which waits for the DB to be up; (2) `alembic upgrade head`, which runs the migrations; (3) `python app/initial_data.py`, which creates the initial data. The backend service waits for prestart to complete successfully before it starts.

The backend reports to Sentry in `staging` and `production`, and only when SENTRY_DSN is non-empty. It does not report when ENVIRONMENT is `local`, which is the default. ENVIRONMENT is limited to `local`, `staging` or `production`. The check is `if settings.SENTRY_DSN and settings.ENVIRONMENT != "local": sentry_sdk.init(...)`.

The frontend image gets `VITE_API_URL` as a build arg, and the value depends on the compose file. In `compose.yml` (production) it is `https://api.${DOMAIN}`, and the build fails if `DOMAIN` isn't set. In `compose.override.yml` (local development) it is `http://localhost:8000`. The override file also builds a separate playwright image with `http://backend:8000`, but that isn't the frontend image.

In nginx.conf, `location /` serves static files from /usr/share/nginx/html with `try_files $uri /index.html =404`. A path that isn't a real file falls back to /index.html, so SPA deep links load the app and the client-side router handles them. The server block also includes /etc/nginx/extra-conf.d/*.conf. The nginx-backend-not-found.conf file defines `location /api`, `/docs` and `/redoc`, and each one does `return 404`. That means those paths return a plain 404 from the frontend container instead of the index.html fallback. I only read the two config files. I didn't check the Dockerfile to confirm that file is mounted into extra-conf.d.
The external Docker network `traefik-public` must exist first. Create it on the remote server with `docker network create traefik-public`.

The dashboard is enabled with `--api`. It is exposed through Traefik's internal service `api@internal`, using a router on host `traefik.${DOMAIN}` over the HTTPS entrypoint (port 443). That router has TLS with a Let's Encrypt certificate from the `le` resolver. The plain HTTP router on port 80 for the same host only redirects permanently to HTTPS, using the `https-redirect` middleware. The HTTPS router is protected by the `admin-auth` middleware, which does HTTP Basic auth with the `USERNAME` and `HASHED_PASSWORD` environment variables. Both variables are required, and compose fails if they are unset.

The staging runner needs the label `staging`. The workflow's `runs-on` is `[self-hosted, staging]`, so the runner is also a self-hosted one. A push or merge to the `master` branch triggers the "Deploy to Staging" workflow, which then runs on it. The job is skipped when the repository owner is `fastapi`, so it only runs in user projects. It builds and starts the stack with `docker compose`, using the `STACK_NAME_STAGING` and `DOMAIN_STAGING` secrets, among others.

For the backend service, `docker compose watch` syncs the `./backend` directory into `/app/backend` in the container. It ignores `./backend/.venv` and `.venv`. It rebuilds the service when `./backend/pyproject.toml` changes.

The local stack (compose.override.yml) publishes these host ports:
- 80 (proxy/Traefik HTTP)
- 8090 (Traefik dashboard, mapped to container port 8080)
- 5432 (db)
- 8080 (adminer)
- 8000 (backend)
- 1080 (mailcatcher web UI)
- 1025 (mailcatcher SMTP)
- 5173 (frontend, mapped to container port 80)
- 9323 (playwright report)

No. The unauthenticated user-creation endpoint is POST /private/users/ (private.py, with no auth dependency). It is registered only when settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local". The production deploy workflow sets ENVIRONMENT=production, and compose.yml passes that value to the backend. So on production the private router isn't mounted and the endpoint isn't reachable. The public /users/signup endpoint is separate and is mounted in every environment.

It's a smoke test that the stack builds and starts. It runs on pushes to master and on PRs (opened/synchronize). The steps are: `docker compose build`, then `down -v` to clean up, then `docker compose up -d --wait backend frontend adminer`. The `--wait` flag waits for those services to be running/healthy. It then curls the backend health check (http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check) and the frontend (http://localhost:5173). Last, it tears everything down. It runs no unit tests. It only checks that the images build, the services start, and the backend and frontend respond over HTTP. Adminer is only checked by `--wait`, with no curl.

In the Test Backend workflow, only the supporting services run in containers. `docker compose up -d db mailcatcher` starts the database and the mailcatcher. Everything else runs directly on the ubuntu-latest runner: checkout, Python and uv setup, DB migration (`uv run bash scripts/prestart.sh`), the tests (`scripts/tests-start.sh`), the coverage upload and the coverage report. The backend app and its tests are not containerized. The workflow runs `docker compose down -v --remove-orphans` before the containers start and again after the tests.

Yes. Local development includes a Traefik proxy with its web UI/dashboard, which shows how routes are handled. It's at http://localhost:8090. compose.override.yml publishes it with "8090:8080" and enables it with --api.insecure=true.

Yes. Stop the backend container with `docker compose stop backend`. Then run `cd backend && fastapi dev app/main.py` to start the local dev server, which reloads on code changes. The local server uses the same ports as the container, so the rest of the stack keeps working.

Install the prek git hook in your local repo. From the `backend` folder, run `uv run prek install -f`. This writes the hook to `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, and the `-f` flag overwrites any existing pre-commit hook. After that, `git commit` runs the checks from `.pre-commit-config.yaml` automatically. If prek reformats or fixes files, stage them again with `git add` and then commit.

Open a shell in the backend container (`docker compose exec backend bash`). Alembic already imports your SQLModel models from backend/app/models.py. Create the migration with `alembic revision --autogenerate -m "Add column last_name to User model"`. Commit the generated file in the alembic directory. Apply it to the database with `alembic upgrade head`.

Edit the local `.env` file and set `DOMAIN=localhost.tiangolo.com`. Then restart the stack with `docker compose watch`. The Traefik proxy in `compose.override.yml` will then route `http://api.localhost.tiangolo.com` to the backend and `http://dashboard.localhost.tiangolo.com` to the frontend. That domain and all its subdomains resolve to 127.0.0.1, so you don't need to change anything else.

Yes. `.vscode/launch.json` has two ready-made debug configurations. "Debug FastAPI Project backend: Python Debugger" runs uvicorn `app.main:app --reload` with debugpy, from the `backend` folder, using the `.env` file. "Debug Frontend: Launch Chrome against http://localhost:5173" launches Chrome against the frontend dev server.

Edit corpus/backend/app/email-templates/src/reset_password.mjml. It holds the body text of the password-reset email: the heading, the "We've received a request…" line, the button label and the footer. The code in backend/app/utils.py renders a built `reset_password.html`. That HTML isn't in the repo, so it's generated from the .mjml file. After editing, rebuild the HTML by exporting the .mjml to `build/reset_password.html` (the MJML VS Code extension does this). The email subject is a separate line, in `generate_reset_password_email` in backend/app/utils.py (line 70).

Yes. `backend/scripts/test.sh` runs `coverage html`, which writes the HTML report to `htmlcov/index.html` under the backend working dir. In the container that is `/app/backend/htmlcov/index.html`. `compose.override.yml` bind-mounts `./backend/htmlcov` to `/app/backend/htmlcov` on the backend service. So on your host you can open `backend/htmlcov/index.html` in a browser. The compose file marks that mount as a TODO to remove once coverage runs locally. It only applies when the override file is used, which is the default for `docker compose`. Note that `scripts/test.sh` runs `docker compose down -v` after the tests. That removes volumes but not the bind-mounted host files, so the report should stay on your host.

The `prestart` service in compose.yml runs `bash scripts/prestart.sh`. That script waits for the DB, then runs `alembic upgrade head`, which creates the tables from the migrations. It then runs `python app/initial_data.py`, which calls `init_db`. `init_db` creates the first superuser from FIRST_SUPERUSER and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD if that user doesn't exist yet. `create_all` in db.py is commented out, so the tables come from Alembic.

The check needs exactly one of these labels on the PR: breaking, security, feature, bug, refactor, upgrade, docs, lang-all, or internal. Ask the maintainer for the one that matches your change. For example, use `bug` for a fix, `feature` for new functionality, or `docs` for documentation. The check is the `label-checker` step, which uses `one_of`. The labeler may add some labels automatically, but the PR still fails until one of these is present.

Use the Appearance menu (components/Common/Appearance.tsx) and pick "Light" (other options: Dark, System); it calls setTheme("light"). Yes, it's remembered: setTheme writes the choice to localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme" and the ThemeProvider reads it back on load. The default, used when nothing is stored, is "dark" (set in main.tsx). The choice is per browser, since it's stored in localStorage.
